cse-1998-a-21.approach: All-pairs shortest paths is solved by Floyd–Warshall, which builds $d^{(k)}$ from $d^{(k-1)}$ by allowing one more intermediate vertex — a textbook dynamic-programming recurrence.

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body:
Let $d^{(k)}_{ij}$ be the shortest $i\to j$ distance using only vertices $1..k$ as intermediates:
$$d^{(k)}_{ij}=\min\left(d^{(k-1)}_{ij},\; d^{(k-1)}_{ik}+d^{(k-1)}_{kj}\right)$$

steps.title: Why it is DP
steps.body: Each table $d^{(k)}$ reuses the overlapping subproblems stored in $d^{(k-1)}$, filled bottom-up in $O(V^3)$ — this is dynamic programming.

optionAnalysis.reason: Floyd–Warshall (and the matrix-multiplication APSP method) are DP over intermediate vertices.
Backtracking explores candidate solutions exhaustively; no standard APSP algorithm uses it.
Greedy (Dijkstra) solves single-source shortest paths; APSP as a technique is the DP formulation.
Divide and conquer splits into independent subproblems; APSP subproblems overlap, which is why DP is used.

pitfalls: Running Dijkstra from every vertex also gives APSP, but the classic APSP design technique asked here is DP.
cse-1998-a-21.verification: Floyd–Warshall is the standard APSP algorithm and is presented in every text as a DP algorithm.

cse-1998-a-32.approach: With $n$ processes each needing at most 2 drives, the worst case is every process holding 1 and waiting for 1; deadlock is impossible if even then one drive is left: $n(2-1)+1\le 6$.

steps.body:

$$n\cdot1+1\le 6 \;\Rightarrow\; n\le 5$$

steps.body: All 6 drives can be held one per process with every process waiting — deadlock. So the maximum is $n=5$.
